# The Week in Public Safety: A Search That Won't End, a Threat That Did, and a Valley Bracing for Water

The call came in at 9:27 on a Sunday morning, one of two injury crashes CHP dispatchers logged within the same minute — the other on Rowlee Road at Kimberlina Road, this one on Keyesville Road, ambulances sent to both. By then, the week in Kern County public safety was already well underway. It would end with a missing woman's 900th day, a school threat that brought police back to campus, and a county staring at a reservoir that has dropped more than 17,000 acre-feet in a month.

## Nine Hundred Days

An Oildale woman is still missing after 900 days, and her daughter is rallying the community in the search for answers, according to 23ABC. That is two and a half years of a case that has not closed — no arrest announced this week, no resolution, just a family still asking. The milestone landed in the same week Bakersfield police asked the public for help in two separate burglary investigations: one in east Bakersfield, one at the Noriega House. In each, the department is searching for a suspect. In the Oildale case, the search has simply gone on longer than most.

## A Threat, a Fire, and a Courtroom

At North High, an online threat prompted increased police presence that will remain in place, 23ABC reported. The district did not treat it as routine, and neither did law enforcement.

In southeast Bakersfield, a woman trapped in a house fire died of smoke inhalation, the coroner determined. The fire itself was reported by KGET 17; the cause of death came later, from the coroner's office.

The week's court docket carried its own weight. A man charged with murder in a deadly shooting at a Mojave Fastrip appeared in court. A woman charged in a crash that killed a Bakersfield couple will receive a developmental disability evaluation. And a judge ruled against Nightingale College in a California nursing license dispute — a case with implications for how nursing programs in the state get credentialed.

## On the Roads

CHP's incident log for the week reads like a map of the county's trouble spots. The Sunday morning cluster alone included the two injury crashes at 9:27, a crash with injuries unknown at 9:20 on Slow Lane, and a crash with no injuries at 3:09 a.m. on an unnamed street. Earlier that morning, at 2:58, a crash with no injuries was reported at Elmo Highway and Browning Road. At 2:27 a.m., a wind advisory went up at Fort Tejon Summit.

The day before brought a traffic hazard at 12:17 a.m. on I-5 northbound just south of Grapevine Road, a traffic advisory at 12:56 p.m. on Compagnoni Street, and a hit-and-run with no injuries at 10:38 a.m. on Easter Street. An animal hazard was reported at 10:10 a.m. on SR-99 southbound just north of Panama Lane. CHP provided traffic control at 9:44 a.m. on I-5 southbound at Lower Water Hole.

None of it was catastrophic. All of it was the ordinary arithmetic of a county where people drive long distances on fast roads, and where the log never stays empty for long.

## Water, and What Comes With It

Isabella Lake sits at 139,691 acre-feet — 24.6 percent of capacity — and has lost 17,415 acre-feet over the past 30 days. That is the backdrop against which Kern County officials are preparing to present plans ahead of possible El Niño impacts, KGET 17 reported. In Pond, residents are bracing for heavy rainfall and possible flooding and say no government help has come. The two stories sit uneasily together: a county getting ready for water, and a community that says it is still waiting.

## The Rest of the Beat

The week's public safety ledger also included a Kern County Sheriff's Office marijuana eradication in Taft — 204 plants seized, one person arrested, per Bakersfield Now, with KGET 17 reporting over 200 plants and one arrest. A volunteer group that describes its work simply — "We drive to save lives" — saved 31 dogs from euthanasia, per 23ABC. A new Angel Walk brought hope to Bakersfield domestic violence survivors, KGET 17 reported.

And in the background, the county kept living: nearly 800 people rallied in Bakersfield for Villegas as the Central Valley congressional race heats up; the Latination art exhibit returned downtown; CSUB business enrollment jumped nearly 25 percent; McFarland Mayor Saul Ayon entered the State Assembly race; a new bike trail along the Friant-Kern Canal neared completion, connecting northwest Bakersfield to the Kern River trail; and Week 10 of high school football rolled on.

## The Through Line

Public safety weeks are usually measured in incidents, and this one had plenty. But the numbers that linger are the ones that don't resolve: 900 days, 24.6 percent, 17,415 acre-feet gone in a month. A daughter still looking. A lake still dropping. A county preparing for rain while some of its residents say the help hasn't arrived yet.
